title: Why the good suffer
hook: the king asks why good people suffer; Nagasena answers carefully

segments.voice: Yesterday, milk to curd: not the same, not another, but it came from the milk. Your line was milk to butter. What in you came from an earlier you? Today, the king's hardest question. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

The king has heard the mango and the milk. Deeds bear fruit; lives grow out of what was planted. So he takes the idea to its edge, where it hurts. The Buddha, he says, had cleared away every unwholesome deed. Then why, in the stories, did he ever suffer? Why did a splinter of rock wound his foot? Why was he ever sick? If every pain is the fruit of something done, the king says, then either the Buddha had bad deeds left, or the teaching is wrong. Pick one. It's a question heard in hospital waiting rooms too: why did this happen to someone who didn't deserve it?
screen: `DEEDS BEAR FRUIT. SO...` → `WHY DID THE BUDDHA SUFFER?` → `PICK ONE, SAYS THE KING.`

segments.voice: First, the careful answer. Nagasena won't pick either. He says the mistake is in the premise: not everything that is felt has kamma as its root. Second, the list. Pain, he says, can come from several causes. From the body's own workings, what the old medicine called wind, bile and phlegm. From the change of seasons. From careless treatment. From a sudden blow from outside. And from kamma. Kamma is one cause among them, not the only one. Those who say every pain is the result of past deeds, he says, go too far. Third, the Buddha's foot. The splinter of rock, Nagasena says, was not the ripening of some old deed. It came from someone else's act and from the plain fact of a stone breaking. The Buddha felt the pain. That did not mean he had earned it. Fourth, why this matters on an ordinary day. It's easy to hear the teaching on kamma as a verdict: you're sick, so you must have done something. Nagasena refuses that reading, in a book the tradition keeps. When someone is suffering, the question 'what did they do to deserve this?' may have no answer at all, because the suffering may not have come from anything they did. Bodies fail. Weather turns. Other people act. Stones fall. That leaves room for something besides judgment. It leaves room to sit beside the person, and to help. The king asked the hard question at full strength, and Nagasena answered without pretending it was easier than it was.
screen: `NOT EVERY PAIN HAS KAMMA AS ITS ROOT.` · `THE BODY, THE SEASONS, A BLOW, KAMMA.` · `THE BUDDHA'S FOOT: PAIN, NOT PAYMENT.` · `ROOM FOR HELP, NOT A VERDICT.` · then, large: `THE HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one unfair thing. Sit still for a moment. Bring to mind something that happened to someone, maybe you, that nobody deserved. You don't need to explain it, and you don't need to fix it in the next two minutes. Just let it be there, without reaching for a reason. If a judgment comes, they must have, I must have, notice it and set it down. Breathe beside it, the way you might sit beside a friend. The bell holds the time.
Kamma. One cause of pain among several, Nagasena says, not the whole story, and not always the reason someone suffers. Today's word.
Your line: the hard question. Today, when you hear of someone's trouble, leave out 'they must have' and ask instead what would help. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers point to this passage of the Questions of King Milinda to say that not all suffering is the result of past kamma, and that illness and accident have other causes too.

fork.setup: you're Nagasena. the king says: if every pain is the fruit of deeds, either the Buddha had bad deeds left, or the teaching is wrong. pick one.
options: the Buddha must have had bad deeds left.
the teaching on kamma is wrong.
neither: not every pain comes from kamma.
fork.reveal: he rejects the premise. pain can come from the body, the seasons, careless treatment, a blow from outside, or kamma: one cause among several.

original.note: Pali: action, deed (Sanskrit karma). in this dialogue, one cause of pain among several, not the only one.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Buddhism, whatever happens to you, you caused.
what it means: Nagasena says not every pain has kamma as its root; the body, the seasons, careless treatment and accident cause pain too.
what a scholar hears: the dilemma turns on the Buddha's own injury and illness; the answer limits kamma's reach rather than stretching it.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 4 (the dilemma of the Buddha's pain: not all feeling has kamma as its root)

notes: The index does not name the passage. I used the dilemma of the Buddha's suffering (the rock splinter, his illness), where Nagasena lists causes of feeling (wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, change of season, careless treatment/'unequal care', external violence, kamma). In Rhys Davids this is in Book 4 (the dilemmas). The count of causes is deliberately not stated. Confirm the list and placement.
The splinter is traditionally from the rock Devadatta hurled; the script says only 'someone else's act'. Confirm.
Keeper may prefer the earlier Book 3 question 'why are not all men alike?' (answered with seeds and kamma); it was not used because it does not fit 'answers carefully' as well.
'Hospital waiting room' hook line is a modern frame; no claim.
Editor: varied the practice opener (same 'settle and let the breath slow' as day 867).
